title: Graph the function
text: Recall the graph of $$y=\cos(x).$$ It is an even function, meaning $$\cos(x)=\cos(-x).$$ How does this affect intervals centered at zero?\n##figure1.gif##

figureAlts.figure1.gif: Graph of the cosine function from negative pi to pi demonstrating even symmetry. The curve mirrors across the y-axis. Key point pairs include: negative pi over three and pi over three both at y equals one-half; negative pi over two and pi over two both at y equals zero; and negative two pi over three and two pi over three both at y equals negative one-half.

title: Check for maxima and minima
text: Check for local extrema (peaks and valleys). If an interval contains a peak or a valley in its interior, the function cannot be $$1-1$$ on that interval.

title: Check the endpoints and the behavior in between
text: On the interval $$[\pi, 2\pi], $$ cosine starts at its minimum $$(-1)$$ and increases monotonically to its maximum (1). This satisfies the $$1-1$$ requirement.\n##figure2.gif##

figureAlts.figure2.gif: Graph of the cosine function over the interval from pi to two pi. The curve is strictly increasing, starting at a minimum of y equals negative one, passing through the x-axis at x equals three pi over two, and reaching a maximum of y equals one at x equals two pi.
